passages.title: Sea Turtles
paragraphs: Sea turtles are reptiles that live in the ocean. In the Philippines, people call them pawikan. Sea turtles have been swimming in the oceans since the time of the dinosaurs.
A sea turtle cannot pull its head and legs into its shell like a land turtle can. Instead, it has strong flippers that help it swim far across the sea.
When it is time to lay eggs, a mother sea turtle crawls onto a sandy beach at night. She digs a hole with her flippers, lays her eggs inside, and covers them with sand. Then she goes back to the sea.
About two months later, the baby turtles hatch. They dig their way out and hurry toward the bright water. Only a few of them will grow up, so it is important to keep beaches clean and safe.

questions.prompt: What do people in the Philippines call sea turtles?
When does a mother sea turtle crawl onto the beach to lay her eggs?
What does the mother turtle do right after she lays her eggs?
Why is it important to keep beaches clean and safe?
options: So more baby turtles can survive

passages.title: Our Moon
paragraphs: On a clear night, the Moon shines brightly in the sky. But did you know the Moon does not make its own light? It shines because it reflects light from the Sun, like a giant mirror.

The Moon travels around Earth. One trip takes about 27 days. As it moves, we see different amounts of its sunny side. That is why the Moon seems to change shape, from a thin crescent to a full, round circle. These shapes are called phases.
The Moon has no air to breathe and no water to drink. Its ground is covered in gray dust and big holes called craters.
In 1969, astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon. His footprints are still there, because there is no wind to blow them away!

questions.prompt: Where does the Moon's light come from?
options: It reflects light from the Sun

questions.prompt: What are the different shapes of the Moon called?
Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
Why are the astronaut's footprints still on the Moon?
options: There is no wind to blow them away

passages.title: The Hardworking Carabao
paragraphs: The carabao is a kind of water buffalo. It is big and strong, with gray skin and long, curved horns. Many people call it the national animal of the Philippines.
For hundreds of years, carabaos have helped Filipino farmers. They pull plows through muddy rice fields and carry heavy loads on carts.
Carabaos love water. On hot days, they lie in mud or rivers to keep cool. The mud also protects their skin from the sun and from biting insects.
Carabao milk is creamy and rich. It is used to make tasty treats like pastillas and kesong puti, a soft white cheese.

questions.prompt: What kind of animal is a carabao?
How do carabaos help farmers?
options: They pull plows and carry heavy loads

passages.title: How Rainbows Are Made
paragraphs: Have you ever seen a rainbow after the rain? A rainbow is a big, colorful arc across the sky.
Sunlight looks white, but it is really made of many colors mixed together. When sunlight shines through tiny raindrops, the drops bend the light and split it into its colors.
A rainbow's colors always appear in the same order: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Some people remember the order with the name ROY G. BIV.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and the rain must be in front of you. If you are lucky, you might even see a double rainbow!

questions.prompt: What is sunlight really made of?
Which color comes right after yellow in a rainbow?
To see a rainbow, where must the sun be?
Why do rainbows usually appear after it rains?
options: Sunlight shines through raindrops still in the air

passages.title: Penguins: Birds That Swim
paragraphs: Penguins are birds, but they cannot fly. Instead, they are amazing swimmers. Their wings work like flippers to help them zoom through the water.
Most penguins live in the southern half of the world. Some live on the icy land of Antarctica, but others live on warmer beaches and islands.
Penguins eat fish, squid and tiny sea animals called krill. A thick layer of fat and tightly packed feathers keep them warm in cold water.

Emperor penguins have a special way of caring for their eggs. The father holds the egg on top of his feet and covers it with a warm fold of skin. He keeps it safe through the freezing winter until the chick hatches.

options: To fly high in the sky

options: A thick layer of fat and tightly packed feathers

passages.title: The Lion and the Mouse
paragraphs: One day, a lion was sleeping in the forest. A tiny mouse ran across his nose and woke him up. The lion grabbed the mouse with his big paw.
"Please let me go!" squeaked the mouse. "If you do, maybe one day I can help you." The lion laughed. How could a little mouse ever help a mighty lion? Still, he let the mouse go.
A few days later, the lion was caught in a hunter's net. He roared and pulled, but he could not get free.

The mouse heard the roar and came running. She chewed through the ropes with her sharp teeth until the lion was free. "You laughed at me," said the mouse, "but even a little friend can be a big help."

options: The lion woke up and grabbed the mouse

options: Even a small friend can be a big help

passages.title: Why We Brush Our Teeth
paragraphs: Every time you eat, tiny bits of food stay on your teeth. Germs in your mouth love to eat these bits, too.
The germs make a sticky layer on your teeth called plaque. Plaque makes acids that can make holes in your teeth. These holes are called cavities, and they can hurt.
Brushing your teeth takes the plaque away. Dentists say you should brush two times a day, for about two minutes each time. Do not forget to brush along your gums and your tongue, too!
Eating fewer sweets, drinking water and visiting the dentist also help keep your smile healthy and bright.

options: Germs feed on sugary food and make acids that cause cavities

passages.title: The Jeepney
paragraphs: If you ride through the streets of the Philippines, you will probably see a jeepney. Jeepneys are colorful vehicles that carry passengers from place to place.

After World War II, American soldiers left many army jeeps in the Philippines. Filipinos made the jeeps longer, added roofs and benches, and turned them into public transportation. That is how the jeepney was born.
Many jeepneys are decorated with bright paint, shiny metal horses, lights and fun designs. No two jeepneys look exactly alike.
Passengers climb in at the back and sit facing each other. They pass their fare to the driver from hand to hand. When they want to get off, they say "Para!" and the driver stops.

options: Army jeeps left after World War II
